newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel says Arafat won't clamp down on "terrorism".
newsitem.headline: Israel says Arafat won't clamp down on "terrorism".

text.p: Israel said on Monday a three-way meeting with the United States and Palestinians had failed to salvage Middle East peacemaking because Palestinian President Yasser Arafat was refusing to clamp down on "terrorism".

U.S. envoy Dennis Ross, within hours of his arrival in the region, arranged for Arafat's first meeting with Israeli officials since a July 30 suicide bomb attack on a Jewish market in Jerusalem deepened a crisis in peace efforts.

But after the meeting in the West Bank town of Ramallah, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's cabinet secretary Danny Naveh told Israel Radio: "We're not interested in meetings for the sake of meetings."

"We very much hope the American envoy Ross's efforts will yield results, but until now we've seen no real change on the part of the Palestinian Authority in everything that has to do with its war on terrorism," Naveh said.

Ross, U.S. President Bill Clinton's special Middle East envoy, separately met both Arafat and Netanyahu twice on Sunday in a bid to ease tensions heightened by the market attack which killed 15 people, including the two bombers.

An official in Arafat's Palestine Liberation Organisation said Ross brought Israeli negotiator Yitzhak Molho, Shin Bet secret police chief Ami Ayalon and a third Israeli with him to a late-night meeting with Arafat.
"The parties have agreed to resume trilateral security meetings...These meetings would pave the way for the political meetings," another PLO official said.
PLO officials said the meeting -- and another scheduled to take place late on Monday -- enabled the sides to exchange information on the attack and to coordinate security.

But Naveh said three-way security meetings had in recent months yielded nothing. He said they had merely enabled Arafat to avoid meeting his responsibility to cooperate directly with Israel on security needs.

In a speech on Sunday, Netanyahu said: "Things will be evaluated not by statements, not by pretty words. Things will be evaluated on the extent to which the Palestinian Authority fulfils their commitments."

Netanyahu has said peace talks will not resume until Arafat arrests militants as he says Arafat pledged to do in peace deals. Naveh said Arafat has a "revolving door" for militants in his prisons. Arafat says he has met his responsibilities.

Mystery has surrounded the origin and identity of the two bombers. The attack, the bloodiest of its kind in Israel for over a year, was claimed within hours in a statement issued in the name of the Islamist group Hamas's military wing.

Netanyahu said on Sunday that Israel had growing indications Hamas -- an opponent of Israeli-PLO peace moves -- carried out the attack even though Israeli and Palestinian officials have questioned the authenticity of the claim.

Negotiations, already in crisis over a Jewish settlement Israel began building in Arab East Jerusalem in March, hit a new low after the market bombing. Netanyahu suspended peace talks and sealed off the West Bank and Gaza.

Arafat wants Israel to stop the East Jerusalem settlement, end Palestinian house demolitions and land confiscations, and lift a closure of the West Bank and Gaza Strip. Israel vows to continue the East Jerusalem settlement.
"I have a sense that there's a desire to find ways to move forward but it will take a lot of work," Ross told Israel's Channel Two television on Sunday.
Ross said U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was prepared to make her first trip to the region at the end of the month provided progress was made on security.

On Sunday Lebanese Shi'ite Hizbollah fighters killed an Israeli soldier, raising to 15 the toll in the deadliest week in south Lebanon since an Israeli offensive in April 1996. A pro-Israeli fighter, six Hizbollah men and seven Lebanese civilians have also died.
